analysis.one_liner: Bans social media accounts for children under 13 and blocks targeted feeds for teens.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan backing on April 30, 2024, the bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a vote or hearing before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit social media platforms from knowingly letting children under 13 hold accounts, require deletion of existing child accounts and their data, and bar platforms from using personalized recommendation systems that feed on young users' personal data for anyone under 17. It would let the FTC and state attorneys general enforce those rules. It would also condition schools' discounted E-Rate internet service on blocking social media on school networks and devices and on adopting grade-by-grade screen time policies.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, and the parents worried about them, would get enforceable limits on platforms' collection of young users' personal data and on accounts held by kids under 13. Schools would get a federal mandate (and public transparency database) around screen time policies, tied to the broadband subsidies many already receive.

how_it_helps.text: Platforms would be barred from knowingly allowing users under 13 to create or keep accounts, must terminate existing child accounts, and must delete the personal data collected from those users, giving the user 90 days to obtain a copy of that data on request.

Platforms could not use personalized recommendation systems that rely on a young user's personal data to suggest or rank content for anyone under 17, except for coarse data like device type, language, city, and age — leaving chronological feeds and direct searches intact.
The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules as an unfair or deceptive practice, and state attorneys general could sue platforms on behalf of residents harmed by violations.

As a condition of receiving discounted internet service through the E-Rate program, schools would have to use filtering technology to block social media on school networks and devices, adopt grade-by-grade screen time policies, and submit them to the FCC, which must publish them in a public database.

analysis.who_pays: Social media platforms would lose ad-targeted engagement from users under 17 and the account base of children under 13. Schools would bear the cost of procuring and operating filtering technology and writing screen time policies, and schools that do not comply would forfeit their E-Rate discounted broadband service.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement is deliberately soft: the bill bars the FTC from requiring age verification or new age collection, so liability turns on what a platform 'knows fairly implied' from objective circumstances — meaning platforms can claim they did not know a user's age, which makes violations hard to prove and gives large platforms wide room to argue compliance.

Tying E-Rate subsidies to social media blocking puts federal broadband money at risk for schools that lag on compliance, and mandated filtering of whole platforms can over-block legitimate educational or teacher-directed uses (the bill exempts sanctioned learning systems and teachers' classroom use, but blunt filters are imperfect).
The school provisions also require monitoring of student network activity to detect social media use, extending surveillance of student online behavior as the price of discounted internet service.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The child-protection provisions address a real and widely felt problem — ad-driven algorithms and accounts targeting young children — and the bill takes care to preserve search, chronological feeds, and educational tools. But its central weakness is that it chose not to require age verification, so its ban on under-13 accounts depends on platforms volunteering knowledge of users' ages; the same companies that profit from young users are the ones who control that knowledge. The school-screen-time title is well-intentioned but adds compliance burden and funding risk for schools in exchange for modest transparency.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on April 30, 2024, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the bill with five cosponsors — three Republicans (Cruz, Britt, Budd) and two Democrats (Murphy, Welch) — on April 30, 2024.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the day it was introduced; the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action at any point afterward.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the bill ever being reported out of committee or voted on, so it died and would need to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Social media platforms are better off: the personalized-recommendation and child-account restrictions that would have cut into their youngest users' engagement and ad targeting never took effect, and no similar federal rule replaced them. Families and schools gained nothing.

for.name: Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Kids Off Social Media Act on April 30, 2024.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 30, 2024, and never held a hearing, markup, or committee vote; the bill never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was split across both parties from day one — a Democratic sponsor joined by three Republicans and two Democrats — and the record shows no partisan opposition; the bill died from inaction, not from a vote.

industries.note: The bill would end under-13 accounts entirely and bar platforms from feeding targeted, data-driven recommendations to anyone under 17 — cutting off the youngest and most engaged segment of their advertising-based business model. Platforms' interest in keeping young users' attention and data runs directly against what the bill was designed to do for children.

industries.industry: School web-filtering and monitoring software vendors
industries.note: Every E-Rate school would need technology that blocks and monitors social media access on school networks and devices, creating a compliance-driven market for filtering vendors. Their gain flows from a child-safety mandate, so it runs alongside the public's interest.

The bill requires deletion of personal data collected from child accounts and restricts use of under-17 personal data in recommendation systems, shrinking the pool of minors whose data can feed ad targeting.
